newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen lower, tobaccos may get boost.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen lower, tobaccos may get boost.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to follow the bond market lower at the open, but Monday's early action will likely center on tobacco and telephone stocks.

"We're back to worrying about the Fed after the durable goods report and release of the minutes of the Fed's meeting," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "It's created a sinking feeling in bonds and in stocks."
Somewhat offsetting the gloomy interest rate picture is some welcome relief for tobacco companies, which emerged victorious in a liability suit last week in Indiana.
Market analysts said the jury verdict could slow a two-week sell-off that has seen Dow industrial component Philip Morris Cos Inc tumble more than a dozen points.
Traders said shares in Philip Morris gained five in pre-open trading to 93 from 88 at Friday's NYSE close. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp rose to 27 in pre-open activity from 25-3/8 on Friday.
Long-distance telephone stocks face a tumultuous day after announcement of a $14 billion merger pact between MFS Communications Co Inc and WorldCom Inc.
Analysts said many telephone stocks could get a boost from the announcement but noted the news could weigh on industry leader AT&T Corp.

"This heats up the merger outlook for other telephone companies," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "but I suspect this will be a little negative for AT&T because the other companies continue to give stiff competition and it seems like they're ganging up here."

In another major telephony deal this morning, MCI Communications Corp announced a significant expansion of its wireless business by agreeing to purchase at least 10 billion minutes of personal communications services capacity from NextWave Telecom Inc over the next ten years.

In Tokyo, stocks closed sharply lower, with the Nikkei-225 index falling 345 points to 20,884. Traders said low volume exaggerated the decline, which was attributed to bouts of arbitrage-linked selling.
A holiday kept markets closed in London.
The dollar was little changed in Tokyo or in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were slightly firmer after a steep fall Friday. The benchmark 30-year bond rose 3/32 to yield 6.95 percent. The S&P 500 index future fell 1.2 to 667.6.
The New York Times Marketplace column examines some of the ways analysts assess the potential legal liabilities faced by tobacco companies.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reports on challenges facing Sun International Hotels Ltd as it attempts to enter Atlantic City's casino market.
